summary:
The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Criminal law and travel-document rules are set at the level of Denmark and extend to the islands, while equality, anti-discrimination and family law are made locally under a Danish human-rights framework.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was decriminalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent for male same-sex relations was then fixed at 18, and the islands did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988.

The islands' anti-discrimination provisions took effect on 1 January 2007. Anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or to imprisonment for up to two years. The measure made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage followed in 2017, late by Nordic standards and after open friction between church and state.

Violence against openly gay people has produced the clearest documented harm. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls. Police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law then banned discrimination against sexual minorities. He was later admitted to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression worsened by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intending to assault them in Tórshavn; nowhere else had the group been attacked.

Petitioning has been a recurring instrument in the territory's disputes. In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; the Faroe Islands had neither at that date, leaving homophobia legally unaddressed. After the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen an internet petition collected 20,000 signatures and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures.

Religiously motivated and official opposition to openly gay public life sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic Prime Minister Johanna Sigurðardóttir and her partner, citing his religion. In 2015, when he demanded that Pride be banned because it fell two days before the national holiday, the singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.

Expression has been a recurring flashpoint. The first gay pride march in 2005 provoked substantial controversy; in June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether these people do not feel any shame. Jenis av Rana repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre.
tangentialFactors:
The 2007 statute positions the Faroe Islands as the last Northern European country to adopt sexual-orientation anti-discrimination protection, and the 2017 marriage law as among the last in the Nordic group. Both milestones arrived decades after Denmark itself.

Opposition is organised rather than marginal: a major party holds formal anti-homosexuality positions, the legislature's speaker publicly attacked the public broadcaster's LGBT coverage, and religious objection was stated as grounds for refusing official hospitality. Public pushback is equally organised, with counter-petitions, large online signature totals relative to a population of roughly 47,000, and prominent cultural figures publicly refusing demands to ban Pride.

The 2006 Rasmussen case indicates a gap between the legal protection adopted in 2007 and the position of police and prosecutors before that date. Whether the current provision has been used to prosecute assault or threats, as distinct from statements, is not addressed by these sources.
localsOnly:
Equality and family law are legislated in the Faroe Islands rather than in Denmark, so residents' protections in employment, services and partnership status derive from local statutes, while the criminal code and document rules applied here are Danish.

The anti-discrimination provision in force since 1 January 2007 covers race, colour, national or ethnic origin and religion alongside sexual orientation, and applies to public statements, with a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. It sits alongside, and does not replace, local policing practice; the Rasmussen case remains the reference point for how complaints of bias violence were handled before it existed.

Political representation of LGBT interests rests on advocacy groups such as LGBT Føroyar and on public campaigning rather than on legislative allies, given the formal position of the Centre Party and the rhetorical role played by senior office-holders.
outOfScopeNotes:
This inventory does not source rules on gender markers or identity documents, entry and visa screening, healthcare or care access, facilities, or the treatment of trans travellers specifically; those elements remain unresolved rather than absent from the jurisdiction.

The prior statement that surveys of the period found violence and discrimination against openly gay people legally unaddressed is not supported by a source in the present inventory and stands unverified here.

Enforcement data for the 2007 provision, including whether the two-year maximum has been applied, is not sourced. Nor is the current status of a registered-partnership mechanism after the 2017 marriage law, or the practical disposition of hate-crime charges distinct from the speech offence described above.
